questions.title: Why does the partition function cancel out when reparameterizing the reward in DPO?
questions.question_body: In the DPO derivation (Equation 12), we express the reward as \(r(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_r(y|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y|x)}+\beta\log Z(x)\). Later, in Equation 13 the partition function \(Z(x)\) disappears. Could someone explain algebraically how exactly the \(\log Z(x)\) terms cancel out when we substitute \(r\) into the Bradley‑Terry preference probability? I want to see the intermediate steps.

questions.title: How does the KL‑constraint in the RL objective translate to a KL‑term between policies in the closed‑form solution?
questions.question_body: Equation 10 shows the optimal policy under a KL‑constrained reward maximizing objective: \(\pi_r(y|x)=\frac{1}{Z(x)}\pi_{ref}(y|x)\exp\frac{1}{\beta}r(x,y)\). What is the intuition behind the term \(\beta\log\frac{\pi_{ref}}{\pi_{ref}}\) appearing in the DPO loss (Equation 15)? How does the KL‑constraint on the policy manifest as a "dynamic importance weight" \(\hat r_\theta(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y|x)}\)?

questions.title: Why is a linear layer added on top of a transformer to predict rewards in the reward‑model phase?
questions.question_body: In the reward‑model phase the paper mentions that the reward network \(r_{\phi}(x,y)\) is initialized from the SFT policy and then a linear layer is added on top of the final transformer layer to output a scalar reward (Section 3.1). What is the justification for this architectural choice? Does it directly correspond to the way the policy logits are used, or is it simply a convenience to produce a single score?

questions.title: How does the Bradley‑Terry model handle ties or equal‑quality responses?
questions.question_body: The Bradley‑Terry probability in Equation 1 assumes a strict preference \(y_1\succ y_2\). In practice, human annotators sometimes label two completions as equally good. How does DPO/ RLHF handle such cases? Is there an extension to the BT model or a separate treatment of the data?

questions.title: What are the implications of the equivalence class of reward functions for policy learning?
questions.question_body: Definition 1 introduces an equivalence relation on reward functions: two rewards are equivalent if they differ by a function of \(x\). Lemma 2 says that equivalent rewards yield the same optimal policy. How does DPO ensure that it does not arbitrarily pick a reward from the equivalence class that might lead to numerical instability? Does this relate to the normalisation of rewards (zero mean) mentioned earlier?

questions.title: Why does DPO need the reference policy \(\pi_{ref}\) and how is it chosen when an SFT model is unavailable?
questions.question_body: The algorithm description says that when an SFT model is not available, \(\pi_{ref}\) is initialized by maximizing the likelihood of the preferred completions: \(\pi_{ref}=\arg\max_\pi \mathbb{E}_{(x,y_w)}\log\pi(y_w|x)\). Could someone elaborate on the intuition behind this choice? How does this relate to the KL‑constraint in the RL objective?

questions.title: How does the dynamic importance weight in the DPO gradient prevent model degeneration?
questions.question_body: Equation 18 shows a weighting term \(\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w))\) in the gradient of the DPO loss. The paper claims that without this weight the model can degenerate. Why does this particular weighting correspond to a form of rejection‑sampling or unlikelihood regularisation? Can we see a simple counter‑example where removing the weight leads to degeneration?

questions.title: How is the hyper‑parameter \(\beta\) chosen and what does it control?
questions.question_body: Throughout the paper \(\beta\) appears as the coefficient of the KL‑entropic term as well as in the DPO loss. In practice, the authors report sweeping over {0.05,0.1,1,5}. What is the theoretical interpretation of these values? How does a large vs. small \(\beta\) affect the trade‑off between staying close to the reference policy and following human preferences?

questions.title: What is the relationship between DPO and the “Best of N” baseline?
questions.question_body: Both DPO and the Best‑of‑N (BoN) approach use the same underlying preference model, but BoN maximises the reward using one‑step sampling. Can we view BoN as a special case of DPO with a particular choice of \(\pi_{ref}\) or \(\beta\)? Why does DPO outperform BoN even though BoN can directly select the highest‑reward sample at inference time?

questions.title: How does DPO generalise to new input distributions compared to PPO‑based RLHF?
questions.question_body: In the out‑of‑distribution experiment (Section 4.3), DPO gives higher win‑rates on CNN/DailyMail news articles than PPO. Is this an artifact of the smaller temperature chosen, or does DPO inherently generalise better? What properties of the DPO objective contribute to this generalisation advantage?

questions.title: Is it possible to apply DPO to multi‑turn dialogue or other reinforcement learning tasks?
questions.question_body: The paper demonstrated DPO on single‑turn dialogue, summarisation and sentiment control. Could DPO be extended to multi‑turn dialogue or tasks that require a long‑horizon reward signal? How would the KL‑constraint and the re‑parameterisation change in that setting?
